title: Active and Passive Voice
notes: What Is Voice?

Voice in grammar refers to the relationship between the subject of a sentence and the action of the verb. Active voice means the subject performs the action (e.g., 'The cat chased the mouse'). Passive voice means the subject receives the action (e.g., 'The mouse was chased by the cat'). Voice is a fundamental concept tested in NEB English exams through transformation exercises, where students must convert active sentences to passive or vice versa.
Structure of Passive Voice

The passive voice is formed using: be (in the appropriate tense) + past participle of the main verb. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence. The original subject (the doer) becomes the agent, introduced by 'by', and can be omitted when it is unknown, unimportant, or obvious. Example: Active — 'Rama wrote the letter.' → Passive — 'The letter was written by Rama.' Key rule: the tense of 'be' must match the tense of the active verb.
Passive Voice in Different Tenses

Present Simple: Active — 'She writes a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter is written by her.' Present Continuous: Active — 'She is writing a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter is being written by her.' Present Perfect: Active — 'She has written a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter has been written by her.' Past Simple: Active — 'She wrote a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter was written by her.' Past Continuous: Active — 'She was writing a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter was being written by her.' Past Perfect: Active — 'She had written a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter had been written by her.' Future Simple: Active — 'She will write a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter will be written by her.' Future Perfect: Active — 'She will have written a letter.' → Passive — 'A letter will have been written by her.'
Passive with Modals

Modal verbs in passive voice follow the pattern: modal + be + past participle. Examples: 'You must finish the work' → 'The work must be finished (by you)'. 'She can swim' → 'Swimming can be done by her' (though this sounds awkward — passives with ability modals are often avoided). 'They should help the poor' → 'The poor should be helped (by them)'. 'He may come late' → 'Late arrival may be expected from him'. This structure is frequently tested in NEB transformation exercises.
Passive with Infinitives and Gerunds

With infinitives: Active — 'I want to see him.' → Passive — 'He is wanted to be seen by me' (rare and awkward, often rephrased). Better: Active — 'They expect him to come.' → Passive — 'He is expected to come.' With gerunds: Active — 'I suggest visiting the temple.' → Passive — 'Visiting the temple is suggested.' Active — 'He denied stealing the money.' → Passive — 'Stealing the money was denied by him.' Note: Passive with gerunds is uncommon in natural English but may appear in academic contexts.
Intransitive Verbs and Passive Voice

Intransitive verbs (verbs that do not take an object) CANNOT be converted to passive voice because passive requires an object to become a subject. Examples of intransitive verbs: arrive, sleep, die, go, come, happen, occur, fall, rise, exist. 'The bird flew' cannot become '___ was flown by the bird.' However, some verbs that are usually intransitive can be used transitively in specific contexts: 'The sun rises' (intransitive) vs. 'She rises the children' (rare/archaic transitive use). Also, intransitive verbs taking a preposition can sometimes be made passive: 'They laughed at him' → 'He was laughed at by them'.
Double Object Verbs in Passive Voice

Some verbs take two objects (a direct object and an indirect object). These can be made passive in two ways: (1) Make the indirect object the subject: Active — 'She gave me a book.' → Passive — 'I was given a book (by her).' (2) Make the direct object the subject: Active — 'She gave me a book.' → Passive — 'A book was given to me (by her).' Both are correct, but the version with the person as subject is more common in everyday English. Other double-object verbs: give, show, tell, send, offer, lend, promise, teach, hand, pass.
Impersonal Passive

The impersonal passive is used with reporting verbs (say, think, believe, know, consider, expect, report) in structures like: 'It is said that...' or 'He is said to...' Active reporting: 'People say that he is rich.' → Passive form 1: 'It is said that he is rich.' → Passive form 2: 'He is said to be rich.' This is a formal structure common in news reports and academic writing. Similarly: 'People believe that she won the prize' → 'It is believed that she won the prize' / 'She is believed to have won the prize.' NEB exams frequently test this transformation.
Causative Passive

The causative passive uses the structure: subject + have/get + object + past participle. It means someone causes something to be done, not necessarily doing it themselves. Example: 'I had my hair cut' (someone cut my hair, not I cut it). 'She got her car repaired' (a mechanic repaired it). This is different from the simple passive 'I was cut' (someone cut me). The causative passive emphasises that the subject arranged for the action to be performed by another person. Common causative verbs: have, get, make.
Passive with Phrasal Verbs

When a verb is followed by a preposition or adverb (a phrasal verb), the preposition/adverb must be retained in the passive. Example: Active — 'They looked after the children.' → Passive — 'The children were looked after (by them).' Active — 'Someone broke into the house.' → Passive — 'The house was broken into (by someone).' Active — 'The teacher pointed out the mistake.' → Passive — 'The mistake was pointed out (by the teacher).' The particle/preposition cannot be dropped — 'The house was broken' changes the meaning entirely.
Verbs That Are Rarely Used in Passive

Some verbs are rarely or never used in the passive voice, even though they are transitive. These include: have (possession), fit, suit, resemble, cost, worth, weigh (when expressing measurement), lack, own, become. For example: 'She has a car' — we do not normally say 'A car is had by her.' 'This shirt fits me' — we do not say 'I am fit by this shirt.' Students should be aware of these exceptions when practising passive transformations.
When to Use Passive Voice

Passive voice is used when: (1) The doer is unknown — 'My bicycle was stolen.' (2) The doer is obvious or unimportant — 'The bridge was built in 1990.' (3) The action is more important than the doer — 'Rice is grown in Nepal.' (4) In formal/scientific writing — 'The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions.' (5) To be tactful or avoid blaming — 'Mistakes were made' (instead of 'You made mistakes'). While active voice is generally preferred for clarity, passive voice has legitimate and important uses in English.
When NOT to Use Passive Voice

Passive voice should be avoided when: (1) The sentence becomes awkward or unclear — 'The ball was hit by the boy' is fine, but 'A letter was being written by me while I was being interrupted by him' is clumsy. (2) The doer is important and known — use active: 'Shakespeare wrote Hamlet' (not 'Hamlet was written by Shakespeare' unless the focus is on the play). (3) The passive makes the sentence unnecessarily long and wordy. (4) In informal writing, where direct, active sentences are more natural and engaging. Active voice is almost always stronger and clearer.
Common Passive Voice Errors

Common errors include: (1) Wrong form of 'be': 'The letter was wrote' (wrong) → 'The letter was written' (right). (2) Omitting the past participle: 'The work is being do' (wrong) → 'The work is being done' (right). (3) Using intransitive verbs: 'He was died yesterday' (wrong — 'die' is intransitive). (4) Wrong tense of 'be': 'The book has been wrote' (wrong) → 'The book has been written' (right). (5) Keeping the original subject: 'By me was written a letter' (wrong word order) → 'A letter was written by me' (right). Regular practice prevents these errors.
Exclamatory and Interrogative Sentences in Passive
confusion: Passive requires a transitive verb: Only verbs that take a direct object can be made passive. 'The child slept' cannot become passive because 'slept' is intransitive. However, 'The child slept the entire afternoon' uses 'slept' transitively (with 'the entire afternoon' as object), making passive possible: 'The entire afternoon was slept by the child' (grammatical but awkward).

Agent omission in passive: The 'by' phrase (agent) is often omitted in passive when the doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. 'The thief was arrested' (we don't know or care who arrested him). 'The novel was written in 1847' (the author is known but irrelevant to the point being made). Including the agent unnecessarily makes the sentence wordy.

Double object passive ambiguity: With sentences like 'They showed me the map,' the passive 'I was shown the map' is clear, but 'The map was shown to me' can be ambiguous — it could mean someone showed the map to the speaker, or someone displayed the map for the speaker to see. Context usually resolves this ambiguity.

Get-passive vs. Be-passive: 'Get' can replace 'be' in passive constructions, especially in informal English: 'He got caught by the police' (instead of 'was caught'). 'Get-passive' often implies the subject was involved in causing the action or that something unexpected happened. It is less common in formal writing but appears frequently in spoken English and NEB-level gap-filling exercises.

Impersonal passive confusion: 'It is said that he is rich' and 'He is said to be rich' mean the same thing, but students often confuse the infinitive forms. Compare: 'People say that he died yesterday' → 'He is said to have died yesterday' (not 'to die' — the perfect infinitive is needed because the dying happened before the saying).

Passive with sense verbs: Sense verbs like see, hear, watch, observe can be used in passive with a bare infinitive or -ing form: 'I saw him cross the street' (completed action) vs. 'I saw him crossing the street' (in progress). Passive: 'He was seen to cross the street' (note: 'to' is required in passive, unlike active). This is a subtle but important distinction tested in advanced grammar exercises.
practice: Change to passive: The cat caught the mouse. [Answer: The mouse was caught by the cat.]
Change to passive: They are building a new bridge. [Answer: A new bridge is being built by them.]
Change to passive: She has finished the work. [Answer: The work has been finished by her.]
Change to passive: Someone stole my bicycle yesterday. [Answer: My bicycle was stolen by someone yesterday. (or: My bicycle was stolen yesterday.)]
Change to passive: The teacher gave the students homework. [Answer: The students were given homework by the teacher. (or: Homework was given to the students by the teacher.)]
Change to passive: They say that he is very honest. [Answer: He is said to be very honest. (or: It is said that he is very honest.)]
Change to passive: Who wrote this poem? [Answer: By whom was this poem written? (formal) or: Who was this poem written by? (informal)]

Change to passive: I had my car repaired. [Answer: This is already passive (causative). No change needed.] — Note: This tests whether the student recognises that the sentence is already in a passive-like structure.
Change to passive: They laughed at the beggar. [Answer: The beggar was laughed at by them.] — The preposition 'at' must be retained.
Change to active: The letter was written by Rama. [Answer: Rama wrote the letter.]
universalFacts: The passive voice exists in many languages but is used much more frequently in English than in languages like French, Spanish, or Nepali. In scientific and academic writing, the passive voice is especially common because it emphasises the research and process rather than the researcher.

In Nepali, the passive voice is formed using the suffix -इने/ -ाइने (e.g., लेख्नु → लेखिन्छ), which has a different structural logic from English passive. Understanding this difference helps Nepali students avoid literal translations like 'I am knowing' instead of 'I know'.

The impersonal passive (It is said that...) is a feature of formal English register. It allows writers to report information without taking responsibility for its truth, a function particularly useful in journalism and academic writing.

George Orwell, in his famous essay 'Politics and the English Language' (1946), argued that passive voice should be avoided because it often hides responsibility: 'The price was raised' (who raised it?) vs. 'The government raised the price' (clear accountability).

The causative passive ('I had my hair cut') is a unique English structure that has no exact equivalent in most languages. It expresses the idea of causing an action to be done rather than performing the action oneself.

In NEB English exams, voice transformation typically carries 3-5 marks. Students are expected to convert simple active sentences to passive and vice versa, including questions and exclamations, within the time limit.
